title: How do you implement soft delete in Hibernate using @SQLDelete, @Where/@SQLRestriction, @Filter, and the newer @SoftDelete? What are the trade-offs?
shortTitle: How do you implement soft delete?

s1_definition.profdef: Soft delete means you never physically remove a row; instead you mark it as deleted (a boolean flag or a deleted-timestamp) and filter it out of normal queries. In Hibernate, `@SQLDelete` rewrites the entity's DELETE into an UPDATE that sets the flag; `@Where` (older) or `@SQLRestriction` (Hibernate 6+) adds a static `WHERE deleted = false` to every query for that entity; `@Filter` is a *dynamic, parameterized* filter you enable per session to optionally include or exclude deleted rows; and `@SoftDelete` (Hibernate 6.4+) is a built-in annotation that wires all of this up automatically. Soft delete preserves history and allows recovery, at the cost of extra filtering and larger tables.
s1_definition.analogy: When National Bank of India "closes" an account, it does not shred the file — regulations require keeping records for years. So instead of destroying the file, the clerk stamps it "CLOSED" and moves it to an archive drawer that is skipped during normal daily work. `@SQLDelete` is the rule that "delete" really means "stamp as closed." `@SQLRestriction` is the standing instruction "when pulling the daily list, ignore anything stamped closed." `@Filter` is a switch the auditor can flip to say "today, include closed files too." `@SoftDelete` is a single pre-approved policy that sets up all of this automatically.
s1_definition.oneliner: Soft delete = mark-as-deleted, not physically remove; @SQLDelete turns DELETE into UPDATE, @SQLRestriction/@Where auto-filters queries, @Filter is a dynamic toggle, @SoftDelete does it all built-in.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Soft delete means you never physically remove a row; instead you mark it as deleted (a boolean flag or a deleted-timestamp) and filter it out of normal queries. In Hibernate, `@SQLDelete` rewrites the entity's DELETE into an UPDATE that sets the flag; `@Where` (older) or `@SQLRestriction` (Hibernate 6+) adds a static `WHERE deleted = false` to every query for that entity; `@Filter` is a *dynamic, parameterized* filter you enable per session to optionally include or exclude deleted rows; and `@SoftDelete` (Hibernate 6.4+) is a built-in annotation that wires all of this up automatically. Soft delete preserves history and allows recovery, at the cost of extra filtering and larger tables.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When National Bank of India "closes" an account, it does not shred the file — regulations require keeping records for years. So instead of destroying the file, the clerk stamps it "CLOSED" and moves it to an archive drawer that is skipped during normal daily work. `@SQLDelete` is the rule that "delete" really means "stamp as closed." `@SQLRestriction` is the standing instruction "when pulling the daily list, ignore anything stamped closed." `@Filter` is a switch the auditor can flip to say "today, include closed files too." `@SoftDelete` is a single pre-approved policy that sets up all of this automatically.

**One line to remember:** Soft delete = mark-as-deleted, not physically remove; @SQLDelete turns DELETE into UPDATE, @SQLRestriction/@Where auto-filters queries, @Filter is a dynamic toggle, @SoftDelete does it all built-in.

sections.s3_banking:
**Problem 1 — a closed account was physically deleted and later needed for an audit.** At National Bank of India, regulators demanded the record of a closed account, but it had been hard-deleted and was gone. Soft delete (mark, do not remove) preserves the record. This is exactly why `@SQLDelete` turns delete into an update.

**Problem 2 — every normal screen must hide closed accounts, but auditors must see them.** Day-to-day lists must exclude closed accounts automatically, yet an audit view needs them. `@SQLRestriction` auto-hides them everywhere, and `@Filter` gives the audit view a runtime toggle to include them. This is exactly the restriction-versus-filter distinction.

What the code will do: an `Account` entity using `@SQLDelete` + `@SQLRestriction` for the default hide-deleted behaviour and a `@Filter` for the audit toggle, with an `AccountService` showing a normal close (soft delete), a normal list (deleted hidden), and an audit list (deleted included).

sections.s5_journey:
Input: close CUR3001 (Priya), then list active accounts, then run an audit list.

Step 1 — `closeAccount` loads CUR3001 and calls `delete`. Because of `@SQLDelete`, Hibernate issues `UPDATE accounts SET deleted = true, deleted_at = now() WHERE id = ?` instead of a physical DELETE. The row and all its data survive for the audit trail.

Step 2 — `listActive` calls `findAll`. Because of `@SQLRestriction`, Hibernate automatically appends `WHERE deleted = false`, so the result contains only SAV2001; CUR3001 is silently excluded even though its row still exists.

Step 3 — the audit path unwraps to a Hibernate Session and enables the `deletedFilter`, binding the parameter. The query then reflects the filter, letting the auditor see deleted rows that the normal path hides.

Step 4 — after the audit query, the filter is disabled so it does not leak into other operations on the same session.

Step 5 — commit. No data was lost; the "deletion" is reversible by flipping the flag back to false.

```
2026-10-24 01:20:02 INFO  Account CUR3001 soft-deleted (row preserved for audit)
2026-10-24 01:20:02 DEBUG Hibernate: update accounts set deleted=true, deleted_at=now() where id=?
2026-10-24 01:20:03 DEBUG Hibernate: select ... from accounts where deleted=false
2026-10-24 01:20:04 INFO  Audit list (deletedOnly=true) returned 1 rows
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  DELETE /accounts/CUR3001
    │
    ▼
  delete(acct)  ──@SQLDelete──→ UPDATE accounts SET deleted=true WHERE id=? (row kept)
    │
    ▼
  GET /accounts (normal)
    │  @SQLRestriction → ... WHERE deleted=false
    ▼
  returns [SAV2001]   (CUR3001 hidden but still in DB)

  GET /accounts?audit (admin)
    │  enableFilter(deletedFilter, isDeleted=true)
    ▼
  returns [CUR3001]   (deleted rows visible)
    │  disableFilter → normal behavior restored
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Soft Delete Annotations (FAANG Level) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Marker-flag / logical delete; Strategy toggle via @Filter  │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: entity owns delete semantics; service owns use cases    │
  │  O: new "include deleted" view = enable filter, no rewrites │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Annotation Roles (as prose) ──
  @SQLDelete     : rewrite DELETE → UPDATE flag (preserve row).
  @SQLRestriction: static WHERE deleted=false on every select (6+); @Where is legacy.
  @Filter        : dynamic, parameterized, enabled per session (audit toggle).
  @SoftDelete    : Hibernate 6.4+ built-in; does all of the above automatically.

  ── State Diagram: account lifecycle ──
  [ACTIVE deleted=false] ─delete()→@SQLDelete─▶ [SOFT-DELETED deleted=true]
         ▲                                              │ restore (flag=false)
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. close → delete() → UPDATE deleted=true
  2. listActive → findAll → auto WHERE deleted=false
  3. audit → enableFilter → see deleted → disableFilter

  (Caution) unique constraints need partial index incl. deleted flag.
  (Caution) native queries bypass @SQLRestriction. (Caution) table bloat → purge job.
  Rule: prefer @SoftDelete on 6.4+; otherwise @SQLDelete + @SQLRestriction + @Filter.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Soft delete means I never physically remove a row; I mark it as deleted with a flag or a timestamp and filter it out of normal queries, which preserves history and allows recovery. In Hibernate I assemble this from a few annotations. The SQL delete annotation intercepts the delete that Hibernate would run and replaces it with my own statement, typically an update that sets the deleted flag, so calling delete on the repository runs an update instead of a physical delete. The SQL restriction annotation, which replaced the older where annotation in Hibernate 6, appends a static predicate like deleted equals false to every select for that entity, so all the normal finders and association loads automatically exclude deleted rows.

The filter annotation is the flexible piece. It defines a parameterized condition that I enable per session with a value, so unlike the static restriction I can decide at runtime whether to include deleted rows, which is exactly what an audit or admin view needs. And the newest option, the soft delete annotation available from Hibernate 6.4, does all of this with a single annotation on the entity: it manages the column, rewrites deletes to updates, and filters selects automatically, so on modern versions I prefer it over manually pairing the SQL delete and restriction annotations.

At National Bank of India this was driven by regulation. A closed account had once been hard deleted and was unavailable for a regulatory audit, so we moved to soft delete to preserve the record. The SQL delete and restriction annotations give us the default behavior where day-to-day screens never see closed accounts, while a filter gives the audit view a runtime toggle to include them. The trade-offs I always raise are that unique constraints need a partial index that includes the deleted flag, because soft-deleted rows still occupy the table and would otherwise block recreating an account; that native queries bypass the restriction and can accidentally return deleted rows; and that soft delete bloats tables and indexes over time, so I pair it with a periodic archival or purge job to move very old deleted records to cold storage.

---

keyPoints: @SQLDelete: override DELETE with UPDATE SET deleted=true
@Where("deleted=false"): filter deleted rows from all queries
@Filter: optional soft-delete filter — can be enabled/disabled
